body: Why not recommend them to use `<!doctype html>`? It's not entirely clear to me what the upside is of creating subtle breakage for the long tail of websites.
@bfgeek do you have example of websites where this is happening? That would be great.

So there are a few reasons why I believe this is good generally for the web platform:
 - Implementations currently are interoperable with each other. We'll get the occasional bug request that we aren't compatible with FF for example (and visa versa). The spec is doing a poor job of handling this at the moment.
 - It makes it difficult to determine what should happen with new features with edge cases like this. For example Igalia is currently working on a line-clamp implementation - and this corner case came up.
 - New implementations (servo/ladybug) wouldn't have to try and reverse engineer what the current implementations are doing if this quirk was reduced/removed.

@karlcow - We don't have a use-counter in place for this - its actually relatively difficult to determine when this would trigger.
Sep 2024 update - we've received some more bug reports with developers getting confused by the margin collapsing quirks.

> Sep 2024 update - we've received some more bug reports with developers getting confused by the margin collapsing quirks.

If this is referring to https://issues.chromium.org/u/1/issues/365516487 (my issue):
The main problem isn't the quirk, the main problem is that your dev tools pretend the quirk doesn't exist and end up showing values that don't line up with the visual behavior on the page.

Also, on the note of usage counting and pages where this is happening:
The header on [this page](http://pa4.pokemonaaah.net/pokemon/index3.html) is rendered in quirks mode in a way that would break if the quirk were to be removed entirely.
It is also already broken in Firefox, but I *think* that's due to differences in the user agent style sheets(?)

I looked into this a bit more and, if I'm not mistaken, the Blink implementation of this part of the spec is currently wrong.
I've made [a web platform test for this](https://github.com/web-platform-tests/wpt/pull/48138) and I suspect that this is the source of at least part of the confusion that developers are facing.

Some more info before the WHATNOT meeting:

I have amended [my web platform test](https://github.com/web-platform-tests/wpt/pull/48138) from September to be a bit more exhaustive in certain edge cases<sup>1</sup>.
The results lead me to believe that Firefox is 100%<sup>2</sup> spec-compliant here.
Chromium "[doesn't really agree with these tests, or that section of the specification](https://github.com/web-platform-tests/wpt/pull/48138#issuecomment-2347318633)", and therefore only passes 8/152 conditions.
(Although visually it produces the correct rendering for a lot more of those, but not all. I'm not sure on the exact numbers, since I haven't checked them all individually.)

A few days ago, I wrote [another passing implementation](https://github.com/LadybirdBrowser/ladybird/pull/3621) for the [Ladybird](https://ladybird.org/) browser.
Writing it (to spec) took absolutely no reverse engineering<sup>3</sup> and ends up matching Firefox's behavior exactly, as far as I can tell.
It also does not rely on any non-standard CSS properties, which is how Firefox does it, and what the Chromium team [seems to take issue with](https://github.com/web-platform-tests/wpt/pull/48138#issuecomment-2347327028).
It does this by simply setting the requried properties on the right elements during the UA stylesheet part of the cascade<sup>4</sup>.
In that way it is somewhat similar to how presentational hints work.

This also means that, for the purpose of implementing new features, the quirk (as specced) should have the same implications as any other quirks mode UA stylesheet rules.

<sup>1</sup> Namely, it now explicitly verifies if specific nodes are substantial/blank or not.
<sup>2</sup> I am not 100% sure about the substantiality of ProcessingInstruction and Comment nodes, but all implementations agree on them either being non-substantial or that there is something in the spec that I am unaware of that causes them to be ignored in that calculation. Either way, good for interop.
<sup>3</sup> bfgeek implied that this would be required in his [post above](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/10296#issuecomment-2224490361)
<sup>4</sup> It currently does this after all the other rules.

Personally, I am in favor of leaving the spec as it is, except if it turns out that all browsers agree on a non-compliant substantiality for ProcessingInstruction and Comment nodes. (they do all agree, I'm just not sure if it is to spec. It seems to be the result of implementing the spec verbatim when I did that for Ladybird, but the specifics of why continue to elude me.)

PS: You can easily run the test in your browser at https://psychpsyo.com/repro/MarginCollapsingQuirks.html

I'll clarify why this part of the specification is bad. So some history - this was initially added in: https://github.com/whatwg/html/commit/c9cef5b83c2786591a771abcbbf8f56a6d5ab866 And the discussion at that time: https://www.w3.org/Bugs/Public/show_bug.cgi?id=15993 The specification was written to match the Firefox implementation - and when added we didn't have as strict policy on other implementations. Typically we try to keep quirks targeted, and small. The specification however doesn't really do this - although it is for the "margin collapsing" quirk (and this is how it works in other implementations), it applies it to *all* margins, even layout modes without collapsing margins. For example: ```

one

two

``` It also affects abspos & float layout which don't participate in margin-collapsing. ```

abspos

``` ```

float

``` (There are more example of this bleeding into other layout modes). Compat wise Safari/Chrome are likely to be the most constrained these days especially on mobile (Firefox has minimal presence there). Practically speaking _expanding_ the quirk as the specification is currently written is a non-starter for us. However happy to try and reduce this quirk still. I suspect we can do this, then after we've reduced (or potentially removed!) we can revisit the cases actually required currently by web compat. We've successfully removed other quirks before such as: https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/8566

> no reverse engineering

I hadn't commented on this, but FWIW I agree with @bfgeek that the more we can constrain these quirks the better. So I don't oppose to simplifying how these quirks work.

Now that I have that context, I agree, this bit of the spec isn't great and reducing the quirk sounds sensible. I've gone ahead and looked for some sites that are affected by this quirk. ### TL;DR: Quirk seems necessary inside TD and BODY, at least for P, and for some others as well. (UL, H1-H3, potentially even FORM, that'd be new) The Firefox/spec definition is not enough. (SCRIPT would need to be non-substantial, margins need to collapse through nesting) Old websites that frequently use table layout are prone to running into this **a lot**. ### Affected Websites: First, http://pa4.pokemonaaah.net/pokemon/index3.html from a previous comment of mine. It \- expects P to lose its top margin inside BODY (that's how I found this) \- expects P to lose its top margin inside TD \- expects SCRIPT to be non-substantial inside TD (broken in Firefox) This is all inside the header in the top left. Breakage is very visible. Clicking around from there, I was able to find http://jajatom.moo.jp/E-top/frame.html. Since [Ladybird](https://github.com/LadybirdBrowser/ladybird) likes to use spec text verbatim as code comments and I wanted to try and implement the 'proper' version of this quirk, I have gone ahead and tried to write a potential spec for the Chromium/Webkit/IE version of this quirk:
(This is written to fit right after [8.3.1 Margin Collapsing](https://www.w3.org/TR/CSS22/box.html#collapsing-margins) in CSS2.2)
<hr>

The **margin-collapsing-quirk-obeying elements** are [blockquote](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-blockquote-element), [dir](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#dir), [dl](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-dl-element), [h1](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-h1,-h2,-h3,-h4,-h5,-and-h6-elements), [h2](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-h1,-h2,-h3,-h4,-h5,-and-h6-elements), [h3](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-h1,-h2,-h3,-h4,-h5,-and-h6-elements), [h4](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-h1,-h2,-h3,-h4,-h5,-and-h6-elements), [h5](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-h1,-h2,-h3,-h4,-h5,-and-h6-elements), [h6](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-h1,-h2,-h3,-h4,-h5,-and-h6-elements), [listing](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#listing), [menu](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-menu-element), [ol](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-ol-element), [p](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-p-element), [plaintext](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#plaintext), [pre](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-pre-element), [ul](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-ul-element) and [xmp](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#xmp).
The **margin-collapsing-quirk-obeying elements with quirky top margins** are [blockquote](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-blockquote-element), [dir](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#dir), [dl](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-dl-element), [h1](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-h1,-h2,-h3,-h4,-h5,-and-h6-elements), [h2](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-h1,-h2,-h3,-h4,-h5,-and-h6-elements), [h3](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-h1,-h2,-h3,-h4,-h5,-and-h6-elements), [h4](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-h1,-h2,-h3,-h4,-h5,-and-h6-elements), [h5](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-h1,-h2,-h3,-h4,-h5,-and-h6-elements), [h6](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-h1,-h2,-h3,-h4,-h5,-and-h6-elements), [listing](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#listing), [menu](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-menu-element), [ol](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-ol-element), [p](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-p-element), [plaintext](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#plaintext), [pre](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-pre-element), [ul](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-ul-element) and [xmp](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#xmp).
The **margin-collapsing-quirk-obeying elements with quirky bottom margins** are any [p](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-p-element) element.

When a Document is in [quirks mode](https://dom.spec.whatwg.org/#concept-document-quirks), vertical margins on [margin-collapsing-quirk-obeying elements]() that are the result of CSS rules which entered the cascade in the [UA-origin](https://drafts.csswg.org/css-cascade-4/#cascade-origin-user) are considered **quirky**.
Of those margins, the top margins on [margin-collapsing-quirk-obeying elements with quirky top margins]() are considered **quirky top margins** and the bottom margins on [margin-collapsing-quirk-obeying elements with quirky bottom margins]() are considered **quirky bottom margins**.

A collapsed margin is considered [quirky]() if all of its component margins are quirky.
If just one of its component margins is not quirky, the entire collapsed margin is not either.
A [quirky]() collapsed margin is a [quirky top margin](), if at least one of its component margins is a quirky top margin.
A [quirky]() collapsed margin is a [quirky bottom margin](), if at least one of its component margins is a quirky bottom margin.
NOTE: This means that a collapsed margin can be both a [quirky top margin]() and a [quirky bottom margin]() at the same time.
If a [quirky top margin]() collapses with a parent's margin that is not also a quirky top margin, behave as if the child margin was not a quirky top margin.
If a [quirky bottom margin]() collapses with a parent's margin that is not also a quirky bottom margin, behave as if the child margin was not a quirky bottom margin.

The margin collapsing quirk causes a margin to have a height of 0 if:
- it is a [quirky top margin]() that is adjoining to the root body element's top margin
- it is a [quirky top margin]() that is adjoining to the top edge of its nearest ancestor td or th element
- it is a [quirky bottom margin]() that is adjoining to the bottom edge of its nearest ancestor td or th element
<hr>

TL;DR:
Any margin that is made up 100% of quirky margins from the UA-stylesheet can collapse away into table cells and the body.
(only the top of the body and there needs to be at least one bottom P margin involved for the bottom of table cells)
When collapsing with a parent's top/bottom margin, the parent's lower quirkiness in that direction wins.

Some extra things to note:
1. This is the Chromium/Webkit version of the quirk. IE is only here for reference and as a curiosity.
That said, I would like it if the FORM element were a **margin-collapsing-quirk-obeying element with quirky bottom margin**, given that there does seem to be some number of pages that expect it to be one.
2. I've chosen to make this care about the nearest ancestor table cell. I don't think this matters right now, but if we were to eliminate the quirk inside TH elements, it might make a difference in nested tables.<sup>[citation needed]</sup>

It might be possible to emulate the quirk and be sufficiently web compatible by using 'margin-trim' on a bunch of elements in quirks.css.

I think it would be worthwhile if we can get interop between browsers and get rid of the "quirky em" unit and Gecko's current apprach (which is closer to what's currently in the spec).

> expands the quirk to all margins, no matter the element or cascade origin

I think this might have some web compat risk. Pages might have author-origin margins and expect them to not be trimmed.

You might not have encountered such pages yet because Ladybird not implementing the quirk is the opposite situation compared to WebKit/Chromium/Gecko switching to `margin-trim`.

I don't think `margin-trim` (as it is currently defined) works for this quirk. A (likely) important part of the work is that: ```

content ``` Is not ignored. Using `margin-trim` would mean that it would. (Part of this quirk has to be done on the individual margins on the elements, so that a web-dev style will override the quirk if set - even if it is the same value - the quirky-em does this by setting a hidden flag on the resulting length).

It'd be nice if we could come up with a version of this quirks that was less invasive that quirky ems to standardize on... Maybe it can be made to work in terms of UA origin? Much like `appearance` works but author-specified backgrounds disable native appearance, author-specified margins would disable quirky margins...

Something like an:

```
-internal-quirky-block-margins: {none,start,both}; /* I don't think we need only quirky end margins? */
```

And in layout the check would be something like:

```
bool HasStartMarginQuirk() const { return (InternalQuirkyBlockMargins() & Start) && !HasAuthorSpecifiedMarginBlockStart(); }
```

Or so, rather than infecting lengths with an extra "quirky" bit...

> It'd be nice if we could come up with a version of this quirks that was less invasive that quirky ems to standardize on... Maybe it can be made to work in terms of UA origin? Much like `appearance` works but author-specified backgrounds disable native appearance, author-specified margins would disable quirky margins...

The potential "chromium version" spec I wrote up above just says that certain margins from the UA origin are "considered quirky".
How a browser does that (qems or not) seems to me like it should purely be an implementation detail and not part of the spec.

> Something like an:
> 
> ```
> -internal-quirky-block-margins: {none,start,both}; /* I don't think we need only quirky end margins? */
> ```

An only quirky end margin would only be needed if we made the quirks-mode-only bottom margin on FORM one.

> And in layout the check would be something like:
> 
> ```
> bool HasStartMarginQuirk() const { return (InternalQuirkyBlockMargins() & Start) && !HasAuthorSpecifiedMarginBlockStart(); }
> ```

Note that something should probably still restrict the quirk to only apply in the vertical direction, just like regular margin collapsing.
(This is the case in Chromium and Webkit right now, but not in Firefox)

It sounds like it ought to be possible for Gecko to get interoperable behavior using a UA-origin-only property instead of qems. I think that would be an improvement.

I'm not convinced that there's much to be gained by removing the quirk for some elements (unless it can be removed completely). It seems like it would make web compat worse. If developers are confused by devtools, maybe devtools can make it clearer (and also highlight and discourage quirks mode more).

I don't have a strong opinion on the `form` end margin. Keeping it non-quirky is a shorter path to interop, but maybe better for web compat to make it quirky.

> It sounds like it ought to be possible for Gecko to get interoperable behavior using a UA-origin-only property instead of qems. I think that would be an improvement.

I still think the spec should not say how to implement this. (at least not in normative text)
Only under what circumstances these margins are expected to collapse away. (coming from the UA stylesheet, adjoining certain parents, etc...)
The rest would be up to the implementation anyways since it wouldn't have any observable effect on the page.

I also think Gecko would need 2 UA-origin-only properties for this, one for the block-start margin and one for the block-end margin since author-specified margins can un-quirk them separately.
No, we should describe something implementable. Not hand-wave it away. As per https://infra.spec.whatwg.org/#algorithm-conformance it can be implemented in other ways.
